content: The function only checks for overlapping busy events and working hours, but it ignores per-person scheduling rules that require buffer time around meetings. The general rule is: availability must account for calendar-specific padding/transition constraints, not just open slots between busy blocks.

The function treats calendar time as only the explicit busy blocks, but real scheduling also has to honor per-person buffer rules and other availability constraints. General rule: when someone requires padding between meetings, you must expand their busy intervals by that buffer before looking for free slots.

The function gets wrong that calendar availability is not just “no overlapping busy events”; some calendars have **required buffer time around meetings** that must be treated as blocked time too. General rule: when scheduling across multiple calendars, always honor attendee-specific padding/transition rules, not just the raw busy intervals.

The function gets wrong the rule that some calendars include **required buffer time around meetings**, not just the meeting’s exact start and end. In general, when an attendee specifies a padding requirement, scheduling must treat the event as blocked with that extra margin on both sides before proposing a time.

The function only checks for raw overlaps with events, but calendars can have extra availability rules like required buffers before/after meetings. The general rule is: when scheduling, treat each attendee’s constraints as expanded busy time, not just the visible event start/end times.

The function ignores attendee-specific buffer rules: it treats meetings as busy only during their exact start/end times, instead of expanding them by the required before/after gap. General rule: availability searches must honor per-person padding/lead-time constraints as part of the blocked interval, especially across time zones.

The function gets the general rule wrong that some calendars impose **buffer time around meetings**: it only checks event overlap, so it can schedule a meeting too close to another one. In other words, it must treat “15 minutes between meetings” as a hard no-start/no-end buffer, not just as a note to ignore.

The function missed a general scheduling rule: availability isn’t just “no overlapping events” — it must also honor per-attendee buffers or spacing requirements around meetings. In calendars like this, those hidden constraints are hard requirements, so a slot can be invalid even when it looks free on the surface.

The function assumes every “time-like” field can be safely split and converted with very rigid string rules, but calendars often store ranges, dates, and offsets in formats that need proper parsing. General rule: calendar logic must be format-tolerant and timezone-aware, not based on brittle string splitting.

The function assumes all calendars use the same clock, so it compares busy times across people without converting time zones. General rule: when attendees are in different UTC offsets, availability must be normalized to one common time zone before searching for shared meeting slots.

The function gets the **calendar-buffer rule** wrong: it only checks whether a slot overlaps busy time, but it doesn’t respect extra spacing requirements around meetings. In general, when scheduling for someone with a buffer policy, you must treat the buffer as part of their unavailable time, not just the meeting itself.

The function gets the **calendar buffer rule** wrong: it treats “free” as simply not overlapping a busy event, instead of also honoring required padding before/after meetings for specific attendees. General rule: when scheduling across calendars, availability must include each participant’s buffer constraints, not just their marked busy blocks.

The function gets the general rule wrong that **availability is not just “no overlapping busy events”** — for some calendars, you must also honor **required buffer time before and after meetings**. In other words, it should treat calendar constraints as **busy time plus any explicit spacing rules**, not simply the event blocks themselves.
